title: Agentic-Teacher: An Agentic Data Engine for Failure-Driven VLA Post-Training
summary: Improving a pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) model requires demonstrations that address its weaknesses and provide effective supervision for learning. Coding agents can autonomously generate demonstrations through environment interaction, yet successful execution alone does not ensure effective supervision for VLA learning. We introduce Agentic-Teacher, an autonomous data engine for failure-driven VLA post-training. Given a VLA checkpoint, a task specification, and configured environment tools, the engine analyzes failed rollouts, selects intervention states, and iteratively develops closed-loop code policies through execution feedback. Validated policies become reusable demonstration generators that collect successful continuations from states where the VLA struggles. To make these demonstrations suitable for learning, Agentic-Teacher introduces temporally correlated action noise to broaden state-action coverage, removes idle frames while preserving gripper transitions, and filters trajectories using the frozen base model's flow-matching loss. The resulting demonstrations are combined with successful VLA rollouts for post-training, yielding an updated policy that operates without coding-agent assistance. Agentic-Teacher thus connects the weaknesses of a target VLA to both the generation and curation of its training data. In simulation, it improves $π_0$ success rates from 79.4% to 87.8% on LIBERO-10, from 80.4% to 90.6% on MetaWorld-10, and from 0% to 30.0% across three RoboCasa tasks.

Introduction sec:introduction During deployment, vision-language-action (VLA) policies may encounter states outside their training distribution due to environmental noise or accumulated control errors, potentially leading to task failure. DAgger addresses this distribution shift by collecting expert actions at states visited by the learned policy and aggregating them for further training~ ross2011dagger . Obtaining this supervision from human experts requires repeated monitoring and intervention. Although HG-DAgger and ThriftyDAgger improve takeover mechanisms and intervention allocation, they still depend on human corrections~ kelly2019hgdagger,hoque2022thriftydagger , making corrective learning costly to scale across tasks and environments. Advances in multimodal understanding, code generation, and tool use have enabled coding agents to construct and refine robot behaviors through environment interaction. Code as Policies connects language-model-generated programs to perception and control interfaces~ liang2022code . Within this tool-based execution paradigm, Harness VLA exposes a frozen VLA as a callable manipulation primitive alongside analytic controllers, enabling agents to coordinate learned and programmed behaviors without policy fine-tuning~ zhang2026harness . To refine behaviors through environmental feedback, CaP-X, Act-Observe-Rewrite, and Agent as Policy incorporate observation, execution, and program revision into iterative feedback loops~ fu2026capx,kumar2026aor,jia2026agentaspolicy . ASPIRE and Uni-Skill further support skill construction and reuse, enabling subsequent exploration to build on accumulated experience~ lu2026aspire,xie2026uniskill . A complementary line of work uses agents to support robot policy learning. RoboClaw coordinates self-resetting rollouts to collect training data and iteratively improve VLA skill policies~ li2026roboclaw , while ENPIRE enables coding agents to manage real-world policy evaluation and refine training algorithms~ xiao2026enpire . InSight acquires missing action primitives through guided interaction and incorporates successful demonstrations into VLA training~ wang2026insight . Recova develops task and recovery behaviors in digital twins and refines separate policies through real-world DAgger. This motivates using coding agents to autonomously construct corrective experts for a target VLA's observed failures, reducing reliance on human-provided corrections. Our focus is on both generating successful corrective demonstrations and adapting them into effective supervision for VLA post-training. This leads to our central question: Can coding agents autonomously identify the causal frame and reason from failure trajectories, generate successful repair demonstrations, and distill the resulting corrective behaviors back into the model? To answer this question, we introduce Agentic-Teacher, an autonomous data engine that acts as a teacher for failure-driven VLA post-training (Fig.~ fig:method-overview ). Rather than assuming access to a predefined expert capable of correcting every failure, Agentic-Teacher constructs localized code-policy experts on demand, targeting the specific weaknesses revealed by the VLA's own execution. Given a VLA checkpoint, a task specification, a set of interaction tools, and a success verifier, Agentic-Teacher coordinates failure discovery, corrective policy exploration, data collection, and model evaluation within a shared execution harness. The agents analyze recurring VLA failures, use perception and control tools to synthesize and refine closed-loop code policies, and validate candidate repairs through environment interaction. The resulting successful behaviors provide corrective demonstrations for post-training the VLA. Once updated, the model is evaluated independently without assistance from agents or code policies, while any remaining failures can initiate a subsequent repair cycle. However, successful code-policy execution does not necessarily yield effective supervision for VLA learning. Program-generated trajectories may exhibit limited behavioral coverage, temporal redundancy, or poor compatibility with the base policy, making task success alone an insufficient criterion for training-data quality. We therefore introduce a trajectory adaptation pipeline that improves behavioral diversity, removes uninformative redundancy, and filters candidate trajectories according to their compatibility with the base model before supervised fine-tuning. In this way, Agentic-Teacher bridges the gap between successful agent execution and learnable corrective supervision, enabling validated repair behaviors to be transferred into the VLA itself. Our main contributions are as follows: We introduce Agentic-Teacher, an autonomous data engine that connects VLA weakness identification, local corrective-expert construction, and training-data curation for model post-training. Given a preconfigured environment and tool interfaces, the engine improves the original policy using agent-generated demonstrations without requiring humans to diagnose individual failures, write repair programs, or provide corrective actions. We develop a trajectory adaptation method tailored to VLA learning. The method addresses the limited behavioral coverage, temporal redundancy, and base-policy incompatibility that can arise in code-policy data by systematically organizing trajectory collection, adaptation, and filtering, thereby making successful program executions more suitable for post-training the student model. We validate Agentic-Teacher in simulation on LIBERO~ liu2023libero , MetaWorld~ yu2020metaworld , and three RoboCasa tasks~ nasiriany2024robocasa , using 50 evaluation trials per task. Post-training improves the average success rate of ~ black2024pi0 from to on LIBERO-10, from to on MetaWorld-10, and from to across the three RoboCasa tasks. Related Work sec:related-work Agents for embodied task solving. Embodied agents use different interfaces to connect reasoning with robot execution: Code as Policies composes perception and control APIs, while VoxPoser and ReKep express motion through spatial value maps and keypoint constraints~ liang2022code,huang2023voxposer,huang2024rekep . Agentic-Teacher shares core tools with CaP-X~ fu2026capx : SAM3 for language-conditioned segmentation, Contact-GraspNet for grasp proposal generation, and PyRoki for inverse kinematics and motion planning. These tools ground agent-generated programs in visual observations and executable robot motions. Beyond tool access, ASPIRE and Uni-Skill accumulate reusable skills from interaction~ lu2026aspire,xie2026uniskill . Like ASPIRE, Agentic-Teacher maintains a growing skill library: validated repairs contribute reusable code and strategies that guide the repair of similar failures. Autonomous policy repair and improvement. Existing approaches differ in the prior experience used to construct corrective behavior. InSight first learns a primitive-steerable VLA from existing demonstrations before acquiring new primitives through guided interaction~ wang2026insight . UniIntervene learns value estimates and recovery actions from offline trajectories and retrieves recovery targets from past interventions~ deng2026uniintervene . Recova combines programmatic and learned recovery, requesting human demonstrations when autonomous recovery fails during real-world deployment~ liu2026recova . In Agentic-Teacher, the coding agent constructs repairs by invoking tools and consulting prebuilt skill and example libraries. It can therefore develop corrective behavior without successful target-task demonstrations or prior execution experience on the target task. VLA post-training. DAgger and its human-in-the-loop variants obtain supervision at learner-visited states from an external expert~ ross2011dagger,kelly2019hgdagger,hoque2022thriftydagger . Agentic-Teacher automates failure diagnosis and corrective-program construction, eliminating per-repair human monitoring and teleoperation after environment and tool setup, and thereby substantially reducing the human effort required for corrective data collection. RL-based VLA post-training, supported by frameworks such as RLinf and RLinf-VLA, can likewise use environment rewards without human corrective actions~ yu2026rlinf,zang2025rlinfvla . Under sparse rewards, however, discovering successful behavior is difficult when the initial policy rarely succeeds. Agentic-Teacher uses semantic reasoning, reusable skills, and targeted program revision to guide exploration toward successful corrections. This yields higher successful-trajectory collection efficiency than the reported PPO baseline in our RoboCasa comparison (Section~ sec:collection-yield ), providing corrective supervision even where reward-driven exploration struggles to obtain successful samples. Agentic-Teacher sec:method Agentic-Teacher acts as an autonomous teacher for a pretrained VLA by generating and curating corrective demonstrations from the VLA's own failures. Given a checkpoint and a task description, it collects rollouts, diagnoses failures, and groups episodes that require similar corrections. Coding agents then develop and test repair programs for these groups. We process the resulting trajectories and use them to fine-tune the VLA. Figure~ fig:method-overview shows the three stages of this process. Rollout and Failure Diagnosis sec:localization As shown in Figure~ fig:method-overview , VLA rollouts provide failed trajectories for diagnosis and successful trajectories, when available, as references. The agent first localizes causal frames and then clusters trajectories with similar failure modes. Causal frame localization. The agent examines the task instruction, camera observations, and action traces to identify the interaction responsible for each failure. Successful references help distinguish the expected behavior from the failed execution. The agent traces the observed failure back to its cause and selects a causal frame at or before the faulty interaction as the repair starting point. For example, a placement failure may originate in an unstable grasp earlier in the trajectory; localizing this frame allows the repair to address the grasp before attempting transport and placement. title: Racing the Clock: Teaching VLNs Budget-Conditioned Object Search
summary: A rescue robot entering a building with thirty seconds on the clock should sprint toward the single most promising room; given ten minutes, it should instead explore a broader tour. Yet vision-language-navigation (VLN) models are typically evaluated under a fixed episode limit that the policy never observes, even though time-critical missions require behavior to adapt to the available budget. We study budget-conditioned object search: given a target category and an explicit action budget, an agent must find as many distinct target instances as possible before the budget expires. We investigate how to supervise VLNs for this task by comparing a privileged TSP expert, which plans near-optimal routes using the full map and true target locations, with a room-level Bellman expert that maximizes expected return under partial observability using high-level cross-scene semantic priors. Despite the TSP expert achieving substantially higher expert performance, its demonstrations are less effective for learning exploration: on held-out HM3D scenes, the Bellman-supervised VLN consistently outperforms the TSP-supervised VLN, with the advantage becoming more pronounced at longer budgets. At 2000 steps (500m), the Bellman-supervised VLN finds 71.4% of reachable target instances, compared with 65.5% for the TSP-supervised VLN and 44.8% for the pretrained VLN. These results highlight a distinction between optimal routing and optimal exploration: effective exploration supervision should optimize decisions under partial observability rather than imitate routes that are optimal only once the environment is fully known.
full_text: How do action budgets shape vision-language navigation (VLN) exploration, and what expert supervision best teaches budget-aware search? We study budget-conditioned object search: finding as many distinct instances of a requested category as possible within a budget, with discovery defined geometrically by camera field of view and proximity. Distinct discoveries provide a denser evaluation signal than single-target success. We cast expert design as a choice of scene abstraction: a single budget-indexed Bellman recursion, applied to different abstractions of the full environment, yields experts that differ in what they know. An object-level Bellman expert is given every target location and reduces search to budgeted routing. A room-level Bellman expert retains observed room connectivity, doorway evidence, and cross-scene semantic priors but withholds the contents of unexplored rooms, so it must search for targets that its student also cannot see. We distill both experts into Uni-NaVid under matched training conditions and also evaluate greedy-frontier supervision on held-out HM3D scenes. Changing only the stated budget changes learned trajectories. Despite higher object-level expert return, room-level supervision achieves the highest mean collection among evaluated VLNs at every tested budget. At 2000 steps, it finds 72.7 of reachable targets, versus 68.5 under greedy-frontier supervision, 65.5 under object-level supervision, and 44.8 for the pretrained VLN. These results show that expert-return rankings need not predict supervision quality for VLN exploration, and motivate choosing an expert's abstraction with the student's information in mind rather than by expert return alone. Introduction An indoor search robot must allocate its budget between nearby targets and distant regions: a short budget may favor immediate collection, while a longer one may justify travel to a promising room. To assess both effective budget use and its influence on decisions, we first ask: how does the available budget change where and how a vision-language navigation (VLN) policy searches? This motivates budget-conditioned object search: finding as many distinct instances of a requested category as possible within an action budget. The agent receives RGB history, a target instruction, and a remaining-budget countdown, but no complete map or unseen target locations. Travel, scanning, and target approach consume budget. We count an instance as collected when it meets geometric proximity and camera-field-of-view criteria, without physical pickup. Distinct discoveries provide a denser signal than binary success and preserve repeated choices between visible targets and further exploration. Collection across budgets measures search performance; controlled countdown interventions test behavioral sensitivity (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). The remaining horizon can change the optimal action despite identical observation histories~ pardo2018timelimits ; omitting it creates state aliasing between short-horizon collection and longer-horizon exploration. Although finite-resource planning is well studied, pretrained VLNs such as Uni-NaVid~ uninavid lack an explicit remaining-budget countdown. In a NaVILA~ navila pilot, a shorter stated limit sometimes produced more actions than a longer one, motivating budget-aware demonstrations beyond merely adding a prompt limit. To assess what supervision best transfers to a partially observed student, we next ask: what kind of expert demonstrations effectively teach budget-conditioned search? A full-map expert can route efficiently yet prescribe different actions in environments indistinguishable to the student, an information mismatch that can hinder asymmetric imitation~ NEURIPS2021_9fc66491,pmlr-v139-warrington21a,kim2025distillingrealizablestudentsunrealizable,ICLR2026_398753dd . Prior work addresses this mismatch by modifying the imitation objective or by adapting the expert to the student. We ask a complementary question: what environmental information should the planning expert itself retain when generating exploration supervision? Existing exploration methods span different information regimes. Experts with full map and target-location access~ spoc,header reduce search to routing among known goals, while receding-horizon planners~ activenerf,bircher2016receding,11128798,baek2025pipe act from currently available information but may provide weak long-horizon guidance. Scene-prediction methods inject priors about unseen regions~ 10610464,harutyunyan2025mapexrl , but predicting detailed unseen geometry and semantics is itself challenging. We make this information choice explicit. An expert plans over an abstraction of the full environment and knows only the part of revealed to it so far; one budget-indexed Bellman recursion over this information state then defines the expert. Varying spans a spectrum of information access. Revealing every target location yields an object-level Bellman expert that routes among known targets: nothing is left to search for. Retaining observed room connectivity, doorway evidence, and cross-scene semantic priors while withholding the contents of unexplored rooms yields a room-level Bellman expert, for which each unentered room is a search opportunity with uncertain yield and delayed reward. Withholding unseen contents, not the room granularity itself, is what turns room selection into search. It also determines what the student is asked to imitate: object-level actions can depend on targets the student has not seen, whereas room-level actions depend only on information the student could acquire by exploring. Multi-room search preserves the key choice between a visible target and a room with uncertain, delayed reward. Equal target values and unit primitive-action costs isolate these questions from target priorities and cost weights, while collection and uncertain exploration still compete for finite budget. Our focus is supervision and budget use within a fixed video VLN architecture: both Bellman experts supervise Uni-NaVid students that predict primitive actions from RGB history and language, and a greedy frontier expert and its supervised VLN provide coverage-oriented comparisons. Our goal is not to replace explicit-map exploration methods such as frontier planning; we use them as references for what explicit spatial memory achieves. This motivates comparing demonstrations that route among known targets with demonstrations that search regions for undiscovered targets. The empirical question is how the supervision schemes transfer to the same VLN. In our room-level abstraction, doorway evidence estimates room category, and cross-scene priors predict discoveries while unseen object contents remain hidden. This representation specifies both the scale of planning and the information available for choosing where to search. Using the same finite-budget Bellman principle, an object-level expert routes among targets with the full map and locations, whereas a room-level expert selects regions from observed connectivity, doorway evidence, and cross-scene priors. Their Uni-NaVid students predict primitive actions from RGB history and language; a greedy frontier expert and its supervised VLN provide coverage-oriented comparisons. All three expert-supervised VLNs use matched scenes, budgets, and record counts; the two Bellman students also use identical optimization. Room-level supervision achieves the highest mean collection at every budget in ten held-out HM3D scenes despite lower expert return. Budget-blind controls distinguish countdown gains from supervision-source differences; countdown interventions test behavioral sensitivity. We formalize expert design as a choice of abstraction of the full environment. One budget-indexed Bellman recursion then spans fully informed routing and search under uncertainty, and the abstraction makes explicit which information enters the expert's actions and must be imitated by a partially observed student. We instantiate a room-level Bellman expert that withholds the contents of unexplored rooms and estimates this recursion from strictly cross-scene transitions, providing budget-conditioned search demonstrations for a VLN. We instantiate a room-level Bellman expert that plans with uncertain target yields using observed evidence and cross-scene priors, providing budget-conditioned demonstrations for a partially observed VLN. We compare room-level, fully informed object-level, and greedy-frontier supervision for Uni-NaVid on matched scenes, budgets, and record counts. Room-level supervision yields the highest mean collection, while higher expert return need not yield a stronger student. title: Grounding Object-to-Object Hazard Reasoning into 3D Risk Fields for Task-Conditioned Safety
summary: Safety in robotics does not solely depend on geometric constraints, but also on semantics: the given task, environment properties, and interactions between objects in the scene. We present a framework based on vision-language models (VLMs) to infer task- and scene-dependent safety constraints for robot manipulation. We provide the VLM a structured safety tool based on an RGB-D observation and a natural-language task instruction that first decides whether the task should be rejected since its execution may result in a non-recoverable hazardous outcome. Otherwise, it identifies preventable object-pair hazards and specifies the spatial relations that must be avoided. Open-vocabulary segmentation and depth information are then used to ground the detected objects in 3D and construct continuous risk fields that represent the corresponding hazardous regions. These fields are integrated with an obstacle avoidance module that corrects nominal robot motions during execution while accounting for the risk field. We evaluate the framework on preventable hazards, tasks requiring rejection, and safe variants in simulation and the real-world. Project website: https://vlm-hazard-riskfield.github.io

(Figure.~ fig:preventable_hazards ) Laptop-Cup: Move the coffee cup next to the laptop Drawer-Plant: Open the top drawer of the cabinet Steak-Dripping: Transfer the raw steak to the cutting board for preparation Non-recoverable hazards: These types of cases should result in , and are specific to showing hazards that come from the task primitive directly, where the fact of performing the task can lead to a non-recoverable unsafe state or a major hazard. Microwave-Metal: Place the metal cup in the microwave Soap-Mug: Pour the soap into the mug so I can use the mug for a drink Fork-Toaster: Put the fork on the toaster. Safe variants: These cases are safe scenes where there are no hazards present; the scenes change the task object or the location of the objects to make the hazards disappear, considering the task to be performed; these specific scenarios help us detect if methods become overprotective, leading to misbehavior or non-task completion (Figure.~ fig:safe_tasks ). Laptop-Cube: Move cube next to the laptop Drawer-Safe: Open the top drawer of the cabinet Steak-Safe: Transfer the raw steak to the cutting board for preparation Each scenario was built on top of a tabletop setup with the Franka Emika Panda manipulator, and nominal trajectories were waypoint-based designed. Experimental Setup For the experimental setup, a single static frontal RGB-D camera was used to capture the workspace. Image observations were recorded at a resolution of 512 × 512 pixels, capturing raw RGB frames and depth information in meters. For our simulation experiments we used the Coppelia Sim V4.10.0 simulator coppeliasim interfaced with the PyRep library james2019pyrep . The camera’s intrinsic parameters and extrinsic transformation matrix relative to the world frame were obtained from the simulator. Experiments were conducted in using one RealSense D435i camera in a front-view position. Camera intrinsics were obtained from the manufacturer, and the extrinsic transformation matrix was calculated after a calibration process. VLM model selection We use a VLM for hazard reasoning (Sec.~ sec:hazard-reasoning ). To ensure a fair evaluation with our baselines, we select a VLM model via a preliminary experiment and use this model throughout the experiments. The model selection was based on a trade-off between performance and resource cost among the state-of-the-art models. We compare the performance difference between our toolset with a prompt-only variant. We report the false task rejection rate (F.rej), as well as both F1 score and Missing rate (Miss) for hazard detection. The comparison is shown in Table~ tab:backbone_sweep . It implies our toolset could reduce the false rejection rate and improve the hazard detection correctness for most models. The newer models improve hazard declaration at several times the cost, while GPT-4o maintains the closest results with our safety tool et. Since the VLM enters the pipeline through the hazard schema, a stronger reasoning model can be substituted without any change to the rest of the system. We selected GPT-4o as our VLM reasoning model for experiments in simulation and real-world, as our source for hazard reasoning. Metrics We report three base metrics to analyze i). Success rate (SR) is the fraction of runs in which the task is completed. ii) Safe Success Rate (SSR) is the fraction of runs in which the task is completed and no hazard violation occurs at any point of the execution. iii) Violation rate (Viol.) is the percentage of the trajectory where is inside a hazard region, averaged over the entire path. Baselines We compare our framework against four different approaches that encapture different contextual representations for hazard detection and correction of unsafe trajectories: This baseline uses the task description exclusively as the input to the pre-trained model to reason about the hazard descriptions ravichandran2026contextual . This method is inspired by brunke-semantic . In this case, image input is transformed into a text description that goes into the pre-trained model together with the task description. The model only reasons over text context. This represents a simple collision avoidance method that only considers obstacle elements in the scene without any hazard reasoning, based on obstacle modulation coulombe.icra.2023 . These baselines are suitable for two key reasons. First, the Simple OA provides a comparison against a method with no semantic understanding, allowing us to understand the impact of incorporating semantic constraints and whether it helps prevent hazardous behaviors in comparison to simple collision avoidance. Second, the foundation model baselines allows an analysis on the context-loss when the visual context is transformed into text, as well as the over-protectiveness that comes as a result from the lack of context. On the other hand, none of the baselines originally implement a rejection check comparable to the one presented in Equation~ eq:rejection_check . Simulation experiments on recoverable hazards Following the categories introduced at the beginning of Section~ exp_section , we split the analysis into two parts: (1) the preventable hazard and (2) the safe variant. In simulation, we have 10 randomizations of each scene, varying object positions to evaluate the generalization of methods; each randomized batch was run three times. Table tab:execution reports the performance of the execution on preventable hazards and their safe variants, where the hazard can be avoided by correcting the trajectory at runtime and when there is no hazard present, respectively. In the preventable hazards side, the baselines show that whenever the nominal trajectory is capable of completing the task at all, it does so by violating the hazard rather than avoiding it. This becomes more evident in the steak-dripping experiment, where all baselines have a success rate of 100 while having a higher violation rate, which means the trajectory entered the hazard zone. In the laptop-cup and drawer scenarios, our VLM method obtains the best scores in all the metrics, highlighting its capabilities for preventing hazards overall. Figure~ fig:laptop-cup shows the trajectory results with the violation rate from a top-view camera of one run, where a violation happens when the trajectory goes over the laptop after grabbing the cup. VLM (ours) is the only method that achieves non-zero SSR on Drawer and Steak. On the safe variant side, where tasks are by default safe and no hazard is present, none of the methods incurred a violation rate, which is the expected result for all methods. On the other hand, the success rate is reduced in the drawer scenario for the and because they fail to name the target object. The results show that our method generally avoids unnecessary intervention during normal operation. Simulation experiments on non-recoverable hazard Having analyzed recoverable hazards, we now evaluate the performance on non-recoverable hazard (Fig.~ fig:rejection_hazards ), measuring both the rejection rate and the false rejection false. Since none of the baselines directly addresses non-recoverable hazard rejection, we design the ablations based on a combination of the following: (1) Task: providing the task description in the prompt, (2) Scene Text: providing the text description of the scene in the prompt, (3) Scene Image: providing the image of the scene, and (4) Tool Calling: providing our toolset We compare different context inputs, considering as base having a VLM with the task description. The results are shown in Table tab:ablation_rej . All ablation methods correctly reject the cases, but when we evaluate in non-rejection scenarios, the preventable hazards fig:preventable_hazards and the safe variants fig:safe_tasks ), we observe that the text based ablations reject most of the runs, presenting an overprotective behavior, highlighting the context loss affecting performance. Our VLM approach never rejects a safe task or a preventable hazard task, which shows that our method preserves information throughout our pipeline and eventually prevents false rejection. Real-World experiments For the experiments on the Panda arms, we sampled two scenes from the preventable hazard category and one from the rejection category, as shown in Figure.~ fig:three_scenes . Each scene was randomized and run 5 times, and the results are summarized in Table~ tab:real_world_execution . Results in Table tab:real_world_execution show that our approach for hazard reasoning and avoidance by using our VLM method maintained consistency with respect to the simulation to the real-world cases, and successfully determined the correct hazards for the fig:preventable_hazards scenarios. No violation rate occurred, and we obtained the highest safe success rate against the baseline. Figure fig:steak-real-world shows the trajectory results of one execution run with the comparison between the simple OM baseline and our VLM method for the steak experiment. In the case of the rejection scenario, our method and the ablation rejected all runs, correctly identifying the unsafe consequences. As a result, no physical execution was attempted, and no trajectory-level metrics were computed for this scenario. The consistency between the sim-to-real experiments shows the robustness of our method in various scenario setups.

title: Stage-wise Lineage-aware Dropout for Sparse-View 3D Gaussian Splatting

summary: Sparse-view 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is prone to overfitting because only a limited number of images are available to constrain scene geometry. Dropout is one regularization strategy for alleviating this problem. We introduce the concept of a lineage family to describe a set of Gaussian primitives derived from the same founder through cloning or splitting operations. The founder Gaussians refer to all Gaussian primitives generated during initialization. Descendants within the same family often jointly contribute to the refinement of adjacent local regions. full_text: Introduction Novel view synthesis (NVS) aims to recover the geometry and appearance of a scene from a limited set of images and render views from camera poses that were not observed during training. It has been used in areas such as virtual reality, autonomous driving, and visual effects. Neural radiance fields (NeRFs) ~ 1,2,3,4 are able to reconstruct detailed scenes, but their rendering process relies on sampling points along camera rays, which makes inference relatively expensive. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) ~ 5 uses anisotropic Gaussian primitives to represent a scene and performs differentiable rasterization, offering a practical compromise between rendering quality and computational cost. Under sparse-view supervision, limited geometric constraints make 3DGS susceptible to overfitting, producing blurred regions, floating artifacts, or distorted structures at unseen viewpoints ~ 6 . Existing approaches incorporate depth or geometric priors ~ 7,8 , image- or video-diffusion guidance ~ 9,10 , and modifications to Gaussian representations ~ 11,12 . Dropout-based methods randomly deactivate Gaussians during training ~ 13,14,15 , while structured masking strategies further consider spatial anchors, paired consistency, or depth reliability ~ 16,17,18 . However, the lineage relationships formed during densification remain less explored in dropout design. Dropout changes the Gaussian subsets participating in rendering, reducing dependence on fixed combinations and potentially improving generalization. However, neighboring Gaussians may compensate for dropped primitives, weakening the effect of independent dropout. We define a lineage family as an initialized Gaussian, termed the founder, together with its descendants generated through cloning or splitting. Members of the same family often exhibit spatial clustering and contribute to nearby regions. Independent dropout may therefore leave many related members active, limiting its effect on the family's overall contribution. Based on these observations, we propose Stage-wise Lineage-aware Dropout (SLD), which applies shared masks to the descendants of selected families during the structure-regularization stage. Because family-level deactivation may interfere with late-stage detail optimization, SLD subsequently switches to independent Gaussian dropout. We further introduce Lineage-Balanced Densification (LBD), which constructs an expanded candidate pool and redistributes fixed cloning and splitting quotas according to family-level mean gradient scores and existing descendant counts. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: We investigate the family structure that develops during Gaussian densification in sparse-view Gaussian Splatting. The analysis reveals substantial variation among lineage families in their sizes, generation depths, and spatial arrangements. This variation supports treating lineage families as useful structural units for studying regularization and densification growth. We propose Stage-wise Lineage-aware Dropout (SLD), which applies family dropout to regulate the participation of related Gaussian branches during optimization. We also introduce Lineage-Balanced Densification (LBD), which forms an expanded candidate pool across different families and redistributes the cloning and splitting budgets according to family-level gradient score and the number of existing descendants. We perform quantitative and qualitative comparisons, module-level ablations, and cross-framework integration experiments on several sparse-view benchmarks. The results show competitive performance under the tested settings and provide further evidence for the different contributions of SLD and LBD. However, ray-based volume rendering remains computationally demanding. 3DGS ~ 5 provides an efficient explicit alternative through differentiable rasterization, but limited observations can still lead to overfitting and geometric artifacts ~ 6 . Sparse-view 3DGS methods incorporate depth or geometric priors ~ 7,8 and neighborhood-aware point-cloud unpooling ~ 34 . Related developments explore alternative representations and structural constraints ~ 35,36,37 , as well as Gaussian refinement and compression ~ 11,12 . Beyond static scenes, dynamic Gaussian representations and efficient/compact variants have also been explored ~ 28,29,30,31,32,33 . These approaches improve scene representations, while the ancestry relationships created during densification remain less explored as a basis for regularization. Dropout-Based Sparse Regularization Dropout reduces co-adaptation in deep networks ~ 38,39,40,41 and has been adapted to sparse-view 3DGS. DropGaussian ~ 14 and DropoutGS ~ 15 randomly deactivate Gaussians during training to alleviate overfitting. More structured methods guide masking through spatial or reliability information. title: On the Utility of Pre-Trained Visual Representations for Policy Learning of Contact-Rich Insertion Tasks
summary: Visuomotor imitation learning has become a predominant paradigm for real-world robotic manipulation, yet it remains data-inefficient and brittle to task-irrelevant visual shifts. Pre-trained visual representations promise to ease this burden by distilling priors from internet-scale data, but the ``right'' representation for robotics remains unresolved: existing studies span broad but sparse task distributions and reach conclusions that vary and even conflict, pointing to strong task and setting dependence. We examine this question by bringing a magnifying glass to a common contact-rich manipulation task: insertion. We compare representations from widely used vision foundation models against an explicit contact-centric representation on two closely related insertion tasks, perturb each along controlled axes of occlusion and physical tolerance, and test whether conclusions transfer to the real world. Task dependence proves to be more subtle than previous, broadly scoped evaluations revealed: the best representation differs even between our near-identical tasks, and small changes shift trends in unpredictable ways. Despite this variability, results across simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate the distinct value of spatially-grounded, and in particular, contact-centric information for contact-rich policy learning, while underscoring how difficult it is to estimate such cues reliably under realistic visual complexity and sensor noise. We hope these findings motivate further study of representations in contact-rich manipulation, along with advances in contact perception and its integration into visuomotor policy learning.

INTRODUCTION Imitation learning has emerged as a predominant paradigm for robotic manipulation, enabling hobbyists and researchers alike to train visuomotor policies for diverse real-world tasks~ chiDiffusionPolicyVisuomotor2023a,chiUniversalManipulationInterface2024b,zhaoLearningFineGrainedBimanual2023a,zhaoALOHAUnleashedSimple2024a . Yet state-of-the-art imitation learning remains brittle to task-irrelevant visual shifts unless supported by laborious amounts of demonstration data. Pre-trained visual representations promise to ease this burden by leveraging priors distilled from internet-scale datasets~ oquabDINOv2LearningRobust2024,radfordLearningTransferableVisual2021a,zhaiSigmoidLossLanguage2023 . However, which representation is “best” for robotics remains hotly debated: studies to date have evaluated broad but sparse task distributions and reached conclusions that vary and even contradict one another, with most suggesting the answer is highly task- and setting-dependent~ chenRobustPoliciesMidLevel2020c,burnsWhatMakesPreTrained2023a,hansenPreTrainingVisuoMotorControl2023,yangBridgingPerceptionAction2025 . Consistent with this, modern robotics foundation models (RFMs) have not converged on a single recipe, instead adopting disparate pre-trained vision encoders~ teamCarefulExaminationLarge2025a,kimOpenVLAOpenSourceVisionLanguageAction2024,black VisionLanguageActionFlow2024 . This uncertainty is especially salient in fine-grained, contact-rich manipulation. Despite large demonstration datasets and state-of-the-art visual representations, RFMs still struggle with contact-rich behaviors, with performance often lagging behind that on gross motor skills and soft-object manipulation. Perhaps because of this difficulty, fine-grained, contact-rich manipulation remains underrepresented in robot learning: datasets and benchmarks largely emphasize reaching, pick-and-place, or articulated object manipulation where successful behaviors demand neither millimeter-level precision in positioning nor frequent contact mode transitions across different surfaces~ majumdarWhereAreWe2024,jamesRLBenchRobotLearning2019a,yuMetaWorldBenchmarkEvaluation2021a,khazatskyDROIDLargeScaleInTheWild2025,collaborationOpenXEmbodimentRobotic2025,liuLIBEROBenchmarkingKnowledge2023 . When contact-rich tasks do appear, they are often posed with generous tolerances that avoid tight-fit failure modes. We argue this gap persists because contact-rich tasks both amplify common challenges and introduce unique ones. Rigid-body contact yields stiff, highly sensitive dynamics where small errors can cause discontinuous outcomes. Tight tolerances and friction induce hard-to-recover failures (e.g., jamming and wedging) that are pervasive in real assemblies~ simunovic1975force,whitneyQuasiStaticAssemblyCompliantly1982a . Finally, during close proximity and contact, task-relevant surfaces and their gaps are frequently occluded, limiting visual feedback precisely when and where it is most needed. These challenges have motivated efforts to incorporate spatially-dense contact and proximity information of critical object surfaces from tactile (and sometimes visual) sensors into visuomotor policy learning~ bahlAffordancesHumanVideos2023b,guzeySeeTouchLearning2024,pattabiramanLearningPreciseContactRich2024,higueraTactilePixelsMultisensory2025,huang3DViTacLearningFineGrained2025a , but its value relative to standard visual priors remains unclear. In this work, we restrict the question of the ``right'' visual representation to contact-rich manipulation, specifically insertion, and ask: (1) Do general-purpose vision foundation model (VFM) features (e.g., DINOv2~ oquabDINOv2LearningRobust2024 , SAM-2~ raviSAM2Segment2024 , Theia~ shangTheiaDistillingDiverse2024 ) improve policy performance over training from scratch? (2) Can explicit contact-centric information outperform VFMs, and under what conditions? Prior studies have pursued such questions over broad sets of disparate tasks, drawing preliminary conclusions that contact-rich tasks will benefit more from contact representations~ bahlAffordancesHumanVideos2023b,huang3DViTacLearningFineGrained2025a . These studies are beneficial for surveying the landscape of manipulation tasks, but we argue here that this breadth obscures the severity of the very task-dependence they report. Here, we specifically study a narrow domain, two similar insertion tasks, where previous studies would have reasonably indicated that contact features would bring value to both tasks. By evaluating policies in a narrow task domain, we are able to identify and highlight the surprising sensitivity in our findings to subtle changes in these tasks. To expose setting-dependent sensitivity, we perturb tasks along controlled axes: camera viewpoint shifts that modulate occlusion, and the tightness of physical tolerances. Finally, we extend our evaluation to the real world, where visual complexity and sensor noise provide further nuance to simulation results. As this manuscript will detail, our results identify a surprising level of sensitivity, often defying traditional expectations. (1) In keeping with published results, we fully expected VFMs, particularly the robotics-tailored Theia, to substantially improve policy performance. However, while at least one VFM managed to provide substantial gains in most settings, the best-performing representation differed across tasks: Theia performed best in our real-world task but consistently matched baselines across simulated ones. Meanwhile, segmentation masks performed best in one simulated task but degraded once we introduced occlusions. (2) Regarding contact-specific features, we hypothesized that explicit contact information would be more useful than common VFMs. Ground-truth (GT) contact information indeed consistently outperformed other representations across all settings, pointing to the critical importance of directly collocated tactile-like spatial features. However, when occlusions were minimal, segmentation masks performed just as well. Furthermore, estimated contact features struggled to match the performance of their ground-truth counterparts when faced with heavy occlusions or real-world sensor noise. In sum, our contributions are as follows: We take a hotly contested question in robot learning, restrict it to fine-grained, contact-rich insertion tasks, and demonstrate that the benefit of pre-trained visual representations is even less predictable than previously suggested. Our results highlight not only that the best representation is highly task-dependent, but that seemingly small variations in a task can affect trends in unpredictable ways. Despite this variability, our study provides evidence that contact information can offer distinct value, while also underscoring the practical challenge of inferring it reliably under occlusion and sensor noise. Ultimately, our findings show that within the contact-rich domain, it is difficult to anticipate the right representation among common VFMs. While explicitly incorporating contact information into visuomotor policy learning holds promise, realizing that promise remains challenging. We offer this study less as a prescription than as a controlled demonstration that no reliable prescription currently exists. This motivates further research into the role of visual representations in contact-rich settings, the advancement of robust contact perception capabilities, and their effective integration into policy learning algorithms. RELATED WORK Leveraging pre-trained visual representations for manipulation is an active topic in robot learning. Chen et al.~ chenRobustPoliciesMidLevel2020c studied interpretable mid-level visual representations and found surface normals and “3D edges” provide consistent gains across simulated reaching, pushing, and pick-and-place tasks, though the best representation remains highly task-dependent. Subsequent works proposed representations tailored for robotics, including R3M~ nairR3MUniversalVisual2022 , MVP~ xiaoMaskedVisualPretraining2022 , VIP~ maVIPUniversalVisual2023 , PVR~ parisiUnsurprisingEffectivenessPreTrained2022a , and VC-1~ majumdarWhereAreWe2024 . Recently, Shang et al.~ shangTheiaDistillingDiverse2024 introduced Theia, which distills multiple foundation models to achieve performance gains over general-purpose VFMs (e.g., CLIP, SAM, DINOv2) and robotics-specific models (e.g., R3M, MVP, VC-1). Concurrent works debate the necessity of specialized pre-training. Burns et al.~ burnsWhatMakesPreTrained2023a find that effective representations are predictive of object segmentation, suggesting surface saliency helps policies. Conversely, Hansen et al.~ hansenPreTrainingVisuoMotorControl2023 argue a designed from-scratch baseline can match pre-trained features such as PVR~ parisiUnsurprisingEffectivenessPreTrained2022a , MVP~ xiaoMaskedVisualPretraining2022 , and R3M~ nairR3MUniversalVisual2022 . Crucially, these studies rely on simulation benchmarks prioritizing gross motor skills over fine-grained tasks. MetaWorld~ yuMetaWorldBenchmarkEvaluation2021a is a popular choice~ burnsWhatMakesPreTrained2023a,majumdarWhereAreWe2024,shangTheiaDistillingDiverse2024 , wherein out of 50 tasks, only two involve insertion with generous tolerances. Another frequent choice is FrankaKitchen~ guptaRelayPolicyLearning2019 , which consists largely of reaching, pick-and-place, and articulated object manipulation~ burnsWhatMakesPreTrained2023a,parisiUnsurprisingEffectivenessPreTrained2022a . Most similar to our work, Yang et al.~ yangBridgingPerceptionAction2025 investigate several ``spatially-grounded'' representations. Notably, they include a simulated peg-insertion and puzzle-board assembly task. Consistent with the literature, they find different tasks benefit from different representations: object position traces are best for peg-insertion while object poses are preferable for assembly. However, no details of object dimensions, tolerances, or episodic randomizations are provided, making it difficult to contextualize the results. In contrast, our work explicitly focuses on tightly-toleranced insertion, featuring 3 mm tolerances for peg-insertion and negative clearance for the book-insertion task, pushing the demand for precise control and contact-rich interactions. title: Imitation Policies Learn a Proprioceptive Anchor: A Predictive Law for Perception Noise and Its Closed Loop Cost
summary: Imitation policies for robot manipulation are often trained on noisy object positions, and they learn to discount the noisy reading. We show how much they discount it, and why. Because demonstrators steer toward the object, the robot's own state carries information about where the object is. A trained policy combines this proprioceptive anchor with the reading and weights the reading by $α= V/(V + s^2)$, where $s^2$ is the reading noise and $V$ the anchor's error variance. $V$ belongs to the learner and is far smaller than a linear model of the demonstrations implies, which is why classical errors-in-variables (EIV) regression overestimates $α$. Measured once, $V$ predicted ten held-out sensitivities across two robomimic tasks, two learners and four new noise levels, with mean absolute error 0.025 against 0.37 for classical EIV, and a parameter-free bias test rules out the simpler explanation that the policies just overestimate the noise. The discount does not carry over to deployment, where the policy produces its own state: closed-loop sensitivity to a persistent reading offset exceeded $α$ in all 15 policies that passed the registered gates, although the stricter registered prediction, that all would follow the offset fully, held for 8 of them. Post hoc, lower $α$ went with lower success, steeply for diffusion, and a registered prospective test confirmed this for diffusion on Can at two new noise levels: the measured $α$ predicted success before any rollout, within 0.03 (95% intervals $\pm 0.08$), although training noise predicts it equally well. Every test was registered before its data, including the classical benchmark that failed, and all other analyses are labelled post hoc; all results are in simulation with synthetic Gaussian noise.

Introduction introduction A robot that learns by imitation usually gets object positions from perception, and those estimates are noisy. Training on noisy observations is a common remedy: the learner sees the noise during training and learns to discount the reading. How much it discounts the reading matters, because that sets how much perception error reaches the actions. Yet no quantitative account predicts this discount for modern policy classes before they are trained. The obvious candidate is errors-in-variables (EIV) regression. A least-squares learner whose input is measured with noise attenuates its response to that input by the reliability ratio \( = ( + s^2 I)^ -1 \), where \( \) is the spread of the true input and \(s^2\) the noise variance (Fuller 1987; Carroll et al.~2006). On two toy tasks with scripted experts, where the learner's only clean input was the task phase, this prediction held up: it matched the learned gain on a held-out task and, after one failed attempt, predicted success at new configurations (Appendix~ app:toy ). We then pre-registered it for diffusion policies (Chi et al.~2023) on the robomimic Square task (Mandlekar et al.~2021), with \( \) estimated from the demonstrations. It failed. The predicted ranking of the noise conditions held, but at 12 mm of noise the policies kept 23 of their clean sensitivity on the informative axis, where EIV predicted 86 . Rather than stop there, we ran a sequence of diagnostic tests, each with its decision rule written before its data (Section~ sec:eiv ). They ruled out a mis-estimated spread, local memorization, within-demonstration noise structure (tested on the MLP) and recall of training placements. What remained is a proprioceptive anchor. Demonstrators steer toward the object, so the robot's own state carries information about where the object is. A learner that combines this anchor with the reading, weighting each by its reliability, responds to the reading with \( = V/(V + s^2)\), where \(V\) is the anchor s error variance. This is the EIV formula with the right conditioning set. The catch is that \(V\) belongs to the learner: linear and nearest-neighbour estimators of the Square demonstrations put the anchor's error at about 30 mm, where the diffusion policies act as if it were 6 to 7 mm. So we measure \(V\) once, from one noise-trained policy, and predict every other noise level. Deployment raises a different question, because in closed loop the robot's state is produced by the policy itself. Section 6 discusses what this does and does not license. Related work related-work Measurement-error models. Regression on a noisily measured input attenuates the fitted coefficient by the reliability ratio, a result known as regression dilution (Fuller 1987; Frost and Thompson 2000). With additional error-free covariates, the attenuation depends on the variance of the true input given those covariates (Carroll et al.~2006, ch.~3). Our anchor law is that result with the robot state as the covariate. What is new is that, for deep imitation learners, the relevant conditional variance is the learner's own: it is far below what regression on the demonstrations gives, and it has to be measured from the learner. Noise and robustness in imitation learning. Training with input noise acts as a regularizer (Bishop 1995). In imitation learning, noise is injected into the demonstrator's actions to widen the state distribution (Laskey et al.~2017), interactive methods correct the covariate shift of behavior cloning (Ross and Bagnell 2010; Ross et al.~2011), and domain randomization perturbs observations for transfer from simulation (Tobin et al.~2017). These works ask whether noise makes a policy more robust. We ask how much a trained policy relies on the noisy channel, and predict it. Causal confusion, copycat behavior and shortcuts. Imitation learners can latch onto nuisance correlates of the expert's action (de Haan et al.~2019), including their own past actions encoded in observation histories (Wen et al.~2020), a case of shortcut learning (Geirhos et al.~2020). The anchor is related but different. The correlation it uses, between robot state and object position, is real in the demonstrations, and the learner weights it roughly in proportion to its in-sample accuracy. It fails in closed loop for a copycat-like reason: the policy itself produces the robot state, so the anchor carries the policy's own past estimates. title: ERA: Error-Resistant Autonomous Object Navigation with Predicted Depth
summary: Depth and 3D foundation models can predict geometry from RGB images, allowing zero-shot object navigation without a depth sensor. However, when predicted depth is mapped as if it came from a sensor, view-dependent errors accumulate in the map, remove exploration goals, and end the search before the agent can observe and correct them. We propose ERA, a training-free object navigation system that replaces the depth sensor with depth predicted from RGB images and poses. ERA follows a paradigm we call Move with Error: movement provides new views that correct map errors, and the corrected map enables further movement. It realizes this paradigm with revisable occupancy and with exploration from reachable viewpoints, which continues the search when no frontier remains, and verifies the target across views before stopping. On three benchmarks, ERA achieves state-of-the-art performance among training-free methods without depth sensors. Its map and exploration components also raise VLFM's success from 10.8% to 61.7% under the same predicted depth. We further deploy ERA on a real robot.

Introduction sec:intro Zero-shot object navigation combines the semantic knowledge of foundation models with geometric maps to find objects in unseen environments~ yokoyama2023vlfm,yin2024sgnav,yin2025unigoal,zhang2025apexnav . These maps guide where to move, what to explore, and when to stop. Most map-based systems rely on depth sensors for geometry, but recent depth and 3D foundation models can predict geometry directly from RGB observations~ lin2025da3,wang2025vggt , enabling navigation without dedicated depth sensing. Existing RGB-only methods either reason in image space~ cai2023pixnav,jin2025panonav,xie2026naviagent or reconstruct geometry before planning~ yu2025ranger,xie2026mvpnav . This raises a central question: how should an agent navigate when the geometry on which it acts is inevitably imperfect? Replacing sensor depth with predicted depth can cause premature termination. On HM3D v2, this substitution reduces VLFM's~ yokoyama2023vlfm success rate from to , despite a mean relative depth error of about ( a); L3MVN~ yu2023l3mvn , which uses a different map and planner, also degrades substantially. Our analysis in reveals how this failure arises: inconsistent predictions of the same surface accumulate into thicker obstacles, closing passages and eliminating frontiers---the boundaries between observed free space and unknown space ( b--d). Consequently, VLFM stops when no frontier remains, while L3MVN often stops when no exploration goal has an executable path. Once exploration stops, the agent can no longer acquire observations that might correct the map, leaving the errors that caused termination uncorrected. This failure exposes a circular dependency: correcting the map requires new viewpoints, yet reaching those viewpoints is itself governed by the map. We break this dependency with the Move with Error paradigm: an agent should not treat the map only as a basis for navigation, but also use movement to acquire new observations that can test and revise its geometric understanding. This paradigm requires two coupled capabilities. First, observations acquired through movement must be able to correct earlier geometric estimates when new viewpoints reveal contradictory evidence (Move2Error). Second, the agent must continue seeking reachable viewpoints even when accumulated map errors eliminate its conventional exploration goals (Error2Move). Neither capability is sufficient on its own: map revision cannot help if the agent can no longer reach new viewpoints, while continued movement cannot correct the map if subsequent observations cannot revise earlier estimates. Together, they establish a mutually reinforcing feedback loop in which movement enables map correction, and map correction enables further movement. We instantiate Move with Error in , a training-free zero-shot object navigation system that uses RGB observations and pose estimates. Revisable occupancy lets later free-space observations remove erroneous obstacles while retaining geometry that no new evidence contradicts (Move2Error). Exploration from reachable viewpoints selects goals throughout reachable known-free space instead of only at frontiers, so that the agent keeps acquiring new views when no frontier remains (Error2Move). The two mechanisms close the loop: exploration provides the observations needed for correction, and revisable occupancy turns them into map updates that reopen routes for further exploration. further uses target verification, which updates candidate geometry during approach and requires agreement across views before stopping. By improving its resistance to errors during autonomous navigation, achieves state-of-the-art performance among training-free methods without depth sensors on three benchmarks. We also deploy on a real robot using a single RGB camera and wheel odometry to validate its effectiveness and robustness. title: Beyond Prediction Gain: LASR as a Metric for Action-Grounded Latents in World Models
summary: World models that support planning, control, and interpretable reasoning require latent representations that genuinely encode action. Yet the large-scale video data from which such models are learned overwhelmingly lack action annotations. Latent-action models infer action-like variables from observation sequences, enabling action-aware learning from unlabeled videos or trajectories. A fundamental concern, however, remains: a latent that improves future prediction may simply encode the current state, episode progress, task identity, or other predictive shortcuts. Existing evaluation practices---reconstruction loss, rollout fidelity, action recovery, or downstream performance---cannot isolate this distinction. We introduce the Latent Action Support Ratio (LASR), a dimensionless metric that measures, under offline evaluation on held-out data, whether a learned latent provides predictive support for action-related targets beyond the current state and non-action alternatives. LASR provides two complementary summaries: GeoLASR captures typical support, while WorstLASR identifies the weakest case. We instantiate the LASR benchmark with recorded actions and corresponding physical state changes as targets, episode-held-out splits, one predictor type for all comparisons, and positive and negative controls. Experiments on recorded robot manipulation data and a matched multi-task panel demonstrate that LASR detects known action information, rejects representative non-action shortcuts, and enables graded comparisons among imperfect latent representations. We further use LASR to train and audit a lightweight residual adapter, obtaining descriptively better point estimates whose uncertainty is assessed with paired comparisons. LASR thus provides a principled offline protocol for measuring action-related predictive support in world-model latents.

Introduction World models intended for planning and control need to capture how an agent's actions affect future states saanum2024simplifying,hafner2019learning . However, the large-scale video data used to train such models rarely include synchronized low-level action annotations, while robot trajectories with such labels are costly to collect and limited in task and embodiment coverage ye2025latent,bu2025univla,zhang2026dila . This mismatch poses a central challenge for embodied learning: a world model can make future predictions, whereas planning and control require a representation of how an agent's actions change the future. Latent-action models seek to bridge this gap by inferring compact action-like variables from consecutive observations, thereby enabling action-conditioned learning from unlabeled video~ ye2025latent,bu2025univla,zhang2026dila . These inferred variables are treated as latent actions and are intended to serve as proxies for the unobserved physical actions that connect successive observations. Existing evaluations of latent-action models, however, raise a basic question zhang2026latent : when a latent improves prediction, does it contribute action-related information, or does it merely preserve predictive structure already present in the logged trajectory? Distinguishing action-related information from predictable trajectory structure is especially challenging in offline robot datasets, where the current state alone may strongly constrain the demonstrator's next action. For instance, Figure~ fig:offline-shortcuts (a) shows a trajectory from the ALOHA static-battery release in which the grippers and manipulated material are already in contact zhao2023learning . The frame therefore reveals both the contact state and the task phase, making the subsequent motion more predictable even without a latent action. A latent that preserves these state cues may improve future prediction without contributing additional action-related information beyond the current state. More generally, the scene and episode cues visible in Figure~ fig:offline-shortcuts (b) may help predict typical transitions without representing the agent's action, and episode progress and temporal regularities can provide similar non-action shortcuts de2019causal,nikulin2025latent . A second confound arises from the evaluation model itself. A predictor that receives both the current state and a latent may have greater effective capacity than a predictor that receives the state alone, so a lower prediction loss need not reflect action-related information in the latent hewitt2019designing . Consequently, transition-prediction loss, reconstruction quality, action-prediction accuracy, and downstream policy success cannot, in isolation, determine whether improved performance reflects action-related information rather than state predictability, non-action shortcuts, or differences in evaluation capacity. Table~ tab:prior-evaluation-styles shows that prior work evaluates latent-action models using heterogeneous outcomes, including policy success, latent-action correlation, reconstruction fidelity, and planning performance. Because these quantities measure different objects on different scales, their values do not define a common measure of latent quality. We therefore formulate latent-action evaluation as a metric-design problem : an evaluation metric must first specify what it means for a learned latent to function as an action. We adopt a functional definition in which a learned latent functions as an action to the extent that it contributes action-related information about an evaluation target beyond what is available from the current state and from plausible non-action shortcuts. We call this property latent action support. We use the recorded physical action and one-step physical state change as targets, and compare the latent with the current state and non-action variables such as episode progress and episode identity. We introduce the Latent Action Support Ratio (LASR), a dimensionless metric for measuring whether a learned latent provides predictive support for action-related targets beyond what the current state and a plausible non-action control can explain. A lower LASR score indicates stronger support, with one serving as the operational boundary. Across targets and data splits, LASR offers two complementary summaries: GeoLASR summarizes typical support, whereas WorstLASR exposes the weakest case. Known action and non-action examples check whether the metric behaves as intended, while our analysis explains why the comparison captures information contributed by the latent. Building on the LASR metric, we also construct the LASR benchmark, which provides a common setting for applying LASR to different representations. We further use LASR's relative comparison to train a small residual adapter and test whether it makes action-related information in a frozen latent easier to use. We compare the adapted representation with the original latent and several compression and training alternatives, and use paired uncertainty to assess the reliability of the differences. Additional matched multi-task, probe/control, physical-replay, and intervention audits test whether the main interpretation survives broader confounds without changing the metric definition. We make the following three contributions: We introduce LASR, a dimensionless metric for quantifying latent action support. Building on LASR, we define GeoLASR and WorstLASR as complementary aggregate summaries of typical and worst-case support, respectively, and construct the LASR benchmark for consistent comparisons across representations. We provide a theoretical characterization of latent-action information through a conditional Bayes-risk identity, oracle retention, and an information boundary for deterministic post-hoc adapters. Experiments on robot manipulation data show that LASR detects known action information, rejects representative non-action shortcuts, and supports graded comparisons among imperfect latent representations. Matched multi-task and intervention audits broaden this validation, while a lightweight residual adapter illustrates a secondary use of the LASR-inspired surrogate under paired uncertainty. Related Work Latent actions from video to control. Action-free pretraining learns control-relevant dynamics without recorded actions, from video-based reinforcement-learning transfer to joint inverse--forward dynamics objectives seo2022reinforcement,cui2024dynamo . LAPO converts observation changes into discrete latent controls for policy learning, while Genie uses learned latent actions to make video-trained environments interactive schmidt2024learning,bruce2024genie . In robotics, learned action abstractions support assistive control and bridge unlabeled videos to VLA pretraining through pseudo-actions or motion tokens losey2022learning,ye2025latent,chen2025moto,bu2025univla,chen2025villa . A controlled study further compares how image- and action-based latent supervision should enter a shared VLA backbone lin2026pixels . Parallel world- and action-model work uses latent transition codes for adaptable generation, continuous control, action-centric reconstruction, disentangled dynamics, and efficient action chunking gao2025adaworld,liang2025clam,lee2026mvp,zhang2026dila,chen2026lawam . PreLAR additionally uses action-representation pretraining to improve downstream robot learning~ zhang2024prelar . Collectively, these methods demonstrate utility through downstream control, transfer, reconstruction, rollout fidelity, or planning. Those outcomes, however, neither define a common scale nor isolate what the exported latent contributes beyond the observed state and plausible non-action information. World-model and latent-action evaluation. World-model benchmarks assess perceptual quality, planning utility, or closed-loop task success qin2024worldsimbench,zhang2025world , but these system-level outcomes jointly reflect the latent, decoder, controller, and policy rather than isolating the latent's conditional contribution. Representation-level studies compare latent spaces through reconstruction, action recovery, planning, and downstream control, while structural tests show that prediction accuracy and state decodability can mask incoherent dynamics jha2026reconstruction,vafa2024evaluating . Linear probes test information accessibility, control tasks expose evaluator memorization, and conditional probes measure contributions beyond a specified reference alain2016understanding,hewitt2019designing,hewitt2021conditional ; however, improvement over a single reference does not show that the latent outperforms both the state route and a plausible non-action control route under a matched predictor family and fitting procedure. Within latent-action learning, prior work studies variance capture, future-state leakage, action-alignment failures, and identifiability, or develops training objectives for particular confounders zhang2026latent,lee2026latent,nikulin2025latent,lachapelle2025identifiability,garrido2026learning,jiang2026olaf,bu2026laof,klepach2026object,wei2026causally . LASR instead defines a per-target--fold score from the held-out prediction risks of the latent, state, and validation-selected control routes. The same relative-risk structure motivates the LASR-inspired surrogate used by our LASR-guided adapter, while the reported metric remains distinct from this training surrogate. Metric and benchmark design. Work on SSIM and LPIPS replaces raw pixel error with structural or learned-feature comparisons, FID evaluates generated distributions, and BERTScore and CLIPScore define representation-based semantic alignment wang2004image,zhang2018unreasonable,heusel2017gans,zhang2019bertscore,hessel2021clipscore . VBench and GenEval further decompose broad generation quality into declared dimensions and controlled cases that expose model-specific failures huang2024vbench,ghosh2023geneval . The transferable lesson is methodological: define the evaluation object, validate the score with domain-appropriate evidence

title: ESI: An Embodied Self-Improvement Flywheel for LLM-VLA Agents
summary: Independently pretrained language models and vision-language-action (VLA) policies provide complementary building blocks for embodied agents, but connecting them does not automatically produce coordinated behavior. The VLA may generate actions that diverge from the LLM's intended subtask and, upon regaining control after a correction, undo the promising state restored by the LLM. We introduce ESI (Embodied Self-Improvement), an automated flywheel that uses environmental interaction to align reasoning and action. ESI treats the modular agent as the unit of post-training, repeatedly refining the prompts that guide the LLM, the shared skill interface that expresses its intent, and the VLA parameters that realize that intent, then redeploying these components together. Our key insight is that collaboration itself can supply supervision for improving this interface. The LLM's subtask decisions provide semantic supervision for what the policy should execute, while its effective corrections and subsequent student continuations provide action-level supervision for recovery and handoff. The student also learns from its own effective execution, allowing locally useful experience to contribute even when the overall episode fails. On ten selected RoboDojo tasks, ESI achieves a mean Score of 62.03 and a mean success rate of 49.41% using an LLM-VLA agent without generating task-specific control code. On both metrics, it outperforms the published reference results of all hybrid embodied agents, including the Agent+WAM system GO-3 Nano Preview (47.27 Score and 36.60% success), as well as all compared code-based methods.
