Introduction sec:intro Robotics is entering a stage in which strong general-purpose reasoning models can participate directly in the control loop. They can interpret unfamiliar instructions, identify relevant objects, reason about intermediate goals, and revise a plan after observing a failure. At the same time, VLA policies provide a powerful substrate for generating continuous robot actions from images, language, and proprioception~ black2025pi0,black2025pi05 . Agentic systems that combine these capabilities are a compelling route toward more general robots: a reasoning model decides what should happen next, and an action model provides the motor behavior needed to make it happen~ ichter2023saycan,shi2025hirobot,gemini2025robotics15,galbot2026gptaspolicy . The central challenge is making this division of labor effective. Both components may be capable in isolation, yet their composition can fail at the interface. A task-finetuned VLA may recognize a familiar scene and reproduce a familiar motion while underusing the teacher's more specific instruction. Related work identifies visual shortcuts that allow scene information to dominate language constraints~ lian2026langforce . A teacher may correctly diagnose a bad approach, adjust the gripper, and restore a promising configuration, only for the student to undo that correction when control returns. These failures expose two closely related gaps: an intent gap between the teacher's decision and the student's behavior, and a handoff gap between the state produced by an intervention and the student's ability to continue. Consider an illustrative packing task. The teacher selects the red object and asks the left arm to grasp it. The student instead approaches another object, or closes its gripper before reaching a suitable contact configuration. The teacher corrects the approach and gives control back. If the student has never learned to act from this corrected state under the intended subtask, it may repeat the original motion or abandon the target. The immediate problem can be solved with more teacher control, but the same coordination failure may recur in the next episode. A system that only intervenes repeatedly spends reasoning effort without necessarily improving its underlying action capability. Our premise is that these interactions are valuable learning data. They identify where the deployed policy diverges from a selected goal, show how that divergence can be corrected, and expose the states from which execution must resume. We therefore treat the reasoning--action interface as a target of collaborative post-training. The teacher remains an online planner, reviewer, and source of corrections. Their joint experience updates the teacher's guidance, the shared skill vocabulary, and the student policy so that future cooperation becomes more effective. This creates a path from episodic assistance to persistent capability. This motivates a shift from model-level to system-level post-training. In a modular embodied agent, decision guidance, the language interface, and motor behavior jointly determine what the system can accomplish. ESI makes their cooperation a learning target: interaction supplies evidence for updating each component, and their joint deployment determines the experience collected next. Through this process, the LLM's scene understanding and corrective judgments become supervision for persistent action capability. Web-to-robot knowledge transfer~ zitkovich2023rt2 and language-guided policy distillation~ ha2023scalingup illustrate how foundation models can support embodied learning. ESI provides a pathway for converting advances in general-purpose foundation models into executable embodied capabilities. This pathway has two stages. During deployment, the LLM contributes scene understanding, planning, and corrective decisions to the current agent. Through the flywheel, effective interaction becomes supervision that updates the action policy and guidance for subsequent rounds. A foundation model thus participates both in performing tasks and in producing the experience from which the embodied system learns. We instantiate this idea in ESI (Embodied Self-Improvement), a configure-once flywheel built on the open-source GPT-as-Policy system~ galbot2026gptaspolicy (Figure~ fig:automation ). During collection, the teacher selects a structured subtask, the VLA proposes an action chunk, and the teacher accepts useful motion or applies a correction. The resulting observations, instructions, reasoning, executed actions, and feedback support round-level updates of decision guidance, the shared skill catalog, and policy parameters. These components are deployed together in the next round, while the LLM's weights remain fixed. The link from interaction to policy improvement is the selection of locally effective behavior. ESI retains successful subtasks from unsuccessful episodes and connects teacher corrections with valid student continuations on the executed timeline. Training under the corresponding local intent teaches the policy both what operation to perform and how to continue from states reached during collaboration. title: Vision-Language-Action Models: A Life-Cycle Survey of Design, Training and Deployment
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt web-pretrained vision-language models to output robot actions, so that web knowledge carries over to physical control. In under 4 years the field has moved from RT-2, the first VLA, to open models that fine-tune on a single consumer GPU and to proprietary generalists that clean unseen homes. This survey reviews 88 works from December 2022 to October 2026, mainly on manipulation and navigation, plus humanoid control, world-action models and evaluation. We follow a VLA through its life cycle, from model design to training and deployment, along seven axes. Model design covers (a) inputs and memory, what the model observes; (b) architecture, how its pipeline is built; (c) action output, how it produces motor commands; and (d) intermediate predictions, what else it predicts, from reasoning steps to future observations. Training covers (e) pretraining data, the mix of robot, web, human and simulated data, and (f) post-training, adaptation to the target robot. Deployment covers (g) real-time execution, keeping pace with the robot. We analyse 22 models on these axes and report their training data, model size, inference speed and hardware. Three trends emerge: (i) training data has broadened, from about 10,000 hours of teleoperated robot data ($π_0$) to 23,000 community-collected episodes (SmolVLA) and 20,000 hours of egocentric human video (GR00T N1.7); (ii) model sizes have split: most recent models have 3-7 billion parameters, while a new group under one billion runs on consumer GPUs; and (iii) generalist VLAs are emerging that handle both manipulation and navigation, such as UniVLA and Qwen-VLA. We also compare VLAs with world-action models, which predict future observations as well as actions. We review evidence that some VLAs with near-perfect benchmark scores fail when objects or the camera move slightly, and open up further research questions.

Introduction Large language and vision-language models (VLMs) acquire broad semantic knowledge from internet-scale data. Robot learning, by contrast, has historically trained a separate policy for each robot, task and environment, using datasets several orders of magnitude smaller. Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect the two. A VLA starts from a pretrained VLM and fine-tunes it to emit actions alongside, or instead of, text. The term was introduced with RT-2~ rt2 , which expressed robot actions as text tokens, co-fine-tuned a VLM on robot trajectories and web data, and showed emergent semantic generalisation. Since then the design space has grown at every stage of a VLA's life cycle. In the model, action heads now range from discrete tokens to diffusion and flow matching, and pipelines from single networks to dual-system and hierarchical designs. In training, data has grown from tens of thousands of teleoperated episodes to tens of thousands of hours of multi-robot experience, supplemented by human video, simulation and the robot's own autonomous attempts. In deployment, models that compute at a few hertz must still control robots smoothly at tens of hertz. This survey has five aims: A life-cycle taxonomy. We organise VLA research along seven design axes that follow a VLA's life cycle, from model design through training to deployment (Section~ sec:taxonomy ), so that a new model can be placed by the choices it makes on each; Table~ tab:axesgrid places 22 main models this way. Manipulation and navigation side by side. Most VLA surveys concentrate on manipulation. We treat navigation VLAs as a parallel lineage (Section~ sec:navigation ), cover locomotion and humanoid whole-body control (Section~ sec:humanoid ), and discuss the recent convergence of manipulation and navigation (Section~ sec:convergence ). A data-centred quantitative view. For every work we extract the training data each paper reports and plot the field's trajectory in robot episodes and in parameter count (Figure~ fig:scaling , Tables~ tab:manip and~ tab:nav ). VLAs versus world-action models, and fair evaluation. We compare VLAs with world-action models (Section~ sec:wam ) and review standard benchmarks and the recent efforts to make VLA evaluation fair and predictive of real-world performance (Section~ sec:benchmarks ). Open problems, including a reporting problem we encountered directly: training data is described in incompatible units, or not quantified at all, in a large share of papers (Section~ sec:challenges ). Figure~ fig:timeline places the main works on a single timeline. Scope and selection. We include works that condition a learned policy on vision and language and produce robot actions or action-level intermediates. Candidates were found by starting from widely used VLAs, following their references and the works that cite them, and searching arXiv; this is a structured, not a systematic, review. A work is discussed in the text if it meets at least one of three criteria: it introduces an original idea, such as a new action representation, architecture or training signal; it makes clear progress on a core problem (manipulation, navigation or locomotion), such as a large gain in real-robot success or a new capability; it gives the community a tool, dataset, benchmark or method that others build on. Works that mainly add a small performance gain or apply an existing method to a new domain are cited but not discussed. We exclude systems announced without method details; version updates described in release notes are included when the base model's method is published (GR00T~N1.5--N1.7). A small number of non-VLA precursors (RT-1, ACT, Diffusion Policy, PaLM-E, Open X-Embodiment) are included because later VLAs build directly on them. The survey covers 88 works from December 2022 to October 2026: 5 foundations, 38 manipulation VLAs, 12 navigation VLAs, 5 surveys, and 28 works on humanoid control, world-action models and evaluation. Preprints are marked with an asterisk ( ) in the tables. Training data is taken from each paper's experiment sections; where a quantity is not reported, we say so. Related surveys. surveyvlaembodiedai gave the first taxonomy of VLAs, with three strands: building blocks, low-level controllers and high-level planners. surveyvlaconceptsprogress cover more than 80 models with an emphasis on applications. surveypurevla classify over 300 studies into autoregressive, diffusion, reinforcement-based and hybrid paradigms. reviewvlarealworld take a full-stack view that includes hardware, data collection and evaluation. openhelixdualsystem survey and empirically compare dual-system architectures. More recent surveys take narrower or different cuts. surveyvlamanipulation divide VLM-based manipulation VLAs into monolithic models, with single- or dual-system designs, and hierarchical models that plan through interpretable intermediates. surveyactiontokenization organise VLAs by the kind of action token they produce, surveyefficientvla review efficiency across models, training and data, and surveyanatomyvla trace VLAs from their modules through milestones to open challenges. On the world-model side, surveyworldmodelrobot review world models for robot learning, surveywam survey world-action models, surveyworldmodelsembodied grade world models by the capabilities that improve behaviour, tutorialwam give a concise tutorial, and surveyunifiedrobotlearning connect representation learning, VLAs and world models in one taxonomy. Our survey differs in four ways: it organises the design space along the life cycle of a VLA and places the main models on it, with a practitioner's guide; it treats navigation and humanoid control as lineages alongside manipulation; it compares world-action models with VLAs from the VLA side; and it extracts training data, model size and inference speed from each paper's full text for a quantitative, data-centred comparison. title: MacroGS: Macro-Pixel Shared Gaussian Primitives for Arbitrary-Scale Light Field Super-Resolutio
summary: Arbitrary-scale light field spatial super-resolution reconstructs high-resolution views at any requested scale from low-resolution multi-view observations. Gaussian primitives enable continuous reconstruction, but generating separate primitive sets for each view redundantly encodes shared scene structure across views and causes the primitive count grow linearly with the number of views. To avoid such redundancy, we propose MacroGS, a feed-forward decoder that jointly predicts a single shared Gaussian set per macro pixel rather than generating separate sets for each view. Disparity-dependent replacement and angle-conditioned appearance allow each set to be reused across all output views, keeping the predicted primitive count independent of the number of views at each requested scale. The decoder iteratively predicts per-primitive disparities, retrieves the corresponding multi-view features, and updates the primitive states. Gaussian splatting and residual refinement then reconstruct the output light field. Despite being learned without geometric supervision, the predicted disparities strongly correlate with underlying scene geometry. Experiments across five benchmarks demonstrate that MacroGS integrates effectively with diverse light field encoders, improving reconstruction quality at fixed scales while achieving leading performance across most evaluated arbitrary-scale settings. The decoder also achieves speedups of approximately $2$-$10\times$ over state-of-the-art implicit light field decoders and $10$-$18\times$ over the view-wise Gaussian baseline.

Introduction sec:intro Arbitrary-scale light field (LF) spatial super-resolution (LFSSR) reconstructs high-resolution sub-aperture images (SAIs) at a requested spatial scale from low-resolution multi-view observations, while retaining the input viewpoint grid. The views observe common surfaces at displaced image locations~ levoy1996 , providing complementary samples for recovering spatial detail~ bishop2012 . Recent encoders aggregate spatial and angular information into low-resolution features~ distgssr,lft,epit,raslf , which a decoder maps to high-resolution views. Fixed-factor upsamplers support only predefined upsampling factors. Coordinate-based implicit decoders allow arbitrary scales by predicting image values from queried coordinates and encoded features~ liif,seiif,saeiif . However, reconstruction requires neural queries over the high-resolution grid of every view. Explicit 2D Gaussian decoders instead predict primitives from image features and splat them at the requested resolution~ gsasr,continuoussr,grape . Each primitive contributes to multiple output pixels, allowing its parameters to be reused across spatial samples. For light fields, common scene structure also motivates sharing primitives across views. A direct extension of a single-image Gaussian decoder applies it separately to each SAI, producing view-specific primitive sets ( a). Even when the input features contain multi-view information, these sets do not share primitive identities or geometric parameters. Common scene structure is therefore parameterized separately, and the primitive count grows with the number of views. We introduce , a feed-forward decoder that jointly predicts Gaussian primitive sets and shares them across output views. It changes the generation unit from an individual SAI pixel to a macro pixel: the samples at one low-resolution spatial coordinate across the views ( b). For each requested scale, a macro pixel generates primitives that all output views reuse. For input SAIs of spatial size , this gives primitives, compared with in a view-wise design with the same per location. Feature reading and rendering still process all views. Joint prediction must account for the fact that macro-pixel samples are not geometrically aligned and may observe different surfaces. Assigning one disparity to the whole macro pixel would force its primitives to share the same cross-view displacement, including at foreground--background boundaries. We instead predict a disparity for each primitive, allowing different displacements within the shared set. Over a fixed number of rounds, the decoder predicts per-primitive disparities, reads features at the implied locations across views, and updates the corresponding primitive states. Disparity thus guides both cross-view feature reading and primitive placement during rendering. Primitive prediction and feature reading operate on the low-resolution grid. Normalized Gaussian splatting renders the shared sets at the requested scale with angle-conditioned appearance, and a residual branch refines the output images. Although the decoder is trained only for image reconstruction, the opacity-weighted means of its predicted disparities correlate strongly with scene geometry. title: Training Reasoning Models in Simulation to Natively Use Real Robots
summary: Robot-use agents (RUAs) have emerged as a promising approach to general-purpose robot control. However, strong performance has so far been achieved only by frontier proprietary models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2, whereas open-weight models remain substantially less capable. We show that an open-weight 27B reasoning model can be trained to use real robots natively through reinforcement learning, entirely in simulation and without demonstrations. Like a computer-use agent (CUA), the model observes the environment, reasons in a chain of thought, and generates the next end-effector pose, without any harness. We build a Post-training Engine for Agentic Robotics (PEAR) and use it to train the model on simulated robot tasks at scale with robot-use reinforcement learning (RURL), mirroring how frontier models acquire computer use. We find that the skills acquired in simulation generalize well beyond the training tasks: they transfer to an unseen robot, to the real world, and to novel instructions. After training on LIBERO and RoboDojo in simulation, the model succeeds in 60% of our trials on a real dual-arm robot, whereas the base model succeeds in none. On LIBERO, training raises the success rate from 1.6% to 74.4%, approaching GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol at maximum reasoning effort. Compared with $π_{0.5}$, a vision-language-action model fine-tuned on demonstrations, our model is substantially more robust to changes in the task itself. On LIBERO-Pro, $π_{0.5}$ succeeds in only 0.75% of episodes when assigned a new task in a familiar scene whereas our model succeeds in 57.4%. Finally, the model retains its general capabilities, with no measurable degradation on nine reasoning, coding and vision benchmarks. These results highlight robot-use reinforcement learning as a promising component of foundation-model post-training.

Introduction sec:intro Robot-use agents (RUAs) have recently become a promising direction for general-purpose robot control~ isola,ora,rpent,aspire . Similar to a computer-use agent (CUA) that operates a computer from screenshots~ cua,claudecu , an RUA uses a vision-language model (VLM) that observes the robot's camera images, reasons about the task, and outputs the next end-effector pose. Because the VLM operates the robot directly, RUAs take advantage of the broad world knowledge and the strong reasoning ability of a capable foundation model, which allows them to generalize and to complete complex tasks. RUAs built on frontier models such as GPT-6 Astra~ gpt6astra,zap,roboicl and Claude Fable 5.2~ fable52 have shown exceptional generalization and language following. On RoboDojo~ robodojo,astrarobodojo and RoboLab~ robolab,astranomy,sensenova , agents built on GPT-6 Astra have outperformed the best previous policies. In contrast, vision-language-action models (VLAs) ~ rt2,openvla,pi0,pi05 fine-tuned on task-specific demonstrations often struggle to generalize to new goals and follow novel instructions~ rl4vla,liberopro,liberoplus,liberocf,liberopara,langgap,igar . Two factors may contribute to the performance of frontier RUAs: the models have been trained for computer use, and they have strong spatial reasoning abilities. We hypothesize that the ability to reason in a chain of thought is particularly important for generalization. However, such performance has so far been obtained only with the strongest proprietary models. Open-weight models have low success rates on the same benchmarks and fail on some simple tasks as well. Several works build a harness that adds skills and components such as the segmentation model SAM~3~ sam3 and turns some motions into a small set of options~ ora,aspire,rpent,openrua,rax,pyrualean,robodojoagent . Such a harness allows open-weight models to complete some of the tasks~ ora , but it may restrict their action space and thereby make other tasks infeasible. As models become more capable, some components of the harness may also be absorbed into the models themselves. Computer-use agents such as OpenAI's are trained with reinforcement learning (RL) on computer tasks~ cua,operatorcard,uitars2 , and the close resemblance between the two settings suggests that robot use could be learned in the same way. We therefore train an open-weight reasoning model with robot-use reinforcement learning (RURL), entirely in simulation and without demonstrations. To support this long-horizon, multi-turn at scale, we build PEAR (a Post-training Engine for Agentic Robotics), an infrastructure designed specifically for training RUAs ( ). In each round, the model observes camera images and the robot’s state, reasons about the task, and outputs the next end-effector pose ( ). Inverse kinematics converts this pose into joint targets, and the robot’s controller executes the movement before the model receives the next observation. Earlier rounds remain in the context, and each episode receives a binary reward indicating whether the task was completed ( ). We provide no perception tools, planners, or skill libraries, so the model itself must localize objects, determine how to manipulate them, and recognize when an action has failed. Because the model specifies poses rather than joint commands and each robot's own inverse kinematics and controller execute them, the same interface applies in simulation and on a real robot. Although the model is trained entirely in simulation, the skills it learns transfer well to the real world. We train the model first on LIBERO~ libero and then on two tasks in RoboDojo~ robodojo . On a real dual-arm robot that it never encountered during training, the model then completes 60 of our trials, whereas the base model completes none ( ). title: Adaptable Watermarking: Transforming Image Watermarking Models via Lightweight Adapters
summary: We explore the adaptability of neural image watermarking models; the extent to which one watermarking method can be transformed into another through lightweight adaptation. We introduce a framework that enables encoder-decoder watermarking architectures to become modular and upgradable, supporting multiple watermarking styles without re-training full models. Adaptation is performed by attaching a compact parameter-efficient adapter and fine-tuning under a multi-domain residual alignment loss (spatial, gradient, and frequency) while preserving bit accuracy via a secret-loss term. We evaluate this approach across a suite of recent watermarking models, including TrustMark, InvisMark, RoSteALS, HiDDeN, and WAM, demonstrating that adapted encoders closely reproduce target residuals and that adapted decoders recover messages with near-optimal accuracy under standard augmentations and distortions. We show that cross-model adaptation, with applications in interoperable and upgradable watermarking, can be achieved with as few as 1-2M trainable parameters per component (e.g., the 2M decoder adapter used in our multi-decoder inference pipeline).

Introduction sec:intro Invisible image watermarking embeds machine-readable signals into images while preserving human visual quality and robustness to common post-processing. It underpins copyright protection, tamper detection, and, increasingly, provenance tracking for AI-generated content Balan-WMF-2023,Collomosse-IEEECGA-2026 . Decades of work have produced a broad toolkit, including classical transform-domain schemes cox1997spread,alhaj2007dwtdct , modern in-generation watermarks for diffusion models yang2024gaussianshading,gunn2025prc,wen2023treering , and watermarking for autoregressive generators tong2025indexmark, jovanovic2025wmar . Surveys highlight that deep learning has become a dominant paradigm across these directions hosny2024survey,zhang2021survey . In this paper, we focus on neural encoder-decoder watermarking for images zhu2018hidden,hosny2024survey,wang2021survey , which are popular for their ability to watermark arbitrary inputs, high robustness, and imperceptibility. To our knowledge, this is the first work to explore neural watermarking methods using parameter-efficient adapters. Numerous architectures have been proposed, including CNN-based models such as TrustMark bui2023trustmark , HiDDeN zhu2018hidden , and StegaStamp tancik2020stegastamp , latent-space designs like RoSteALS bui2023rosteals , and transformer-based or segmentation-aware models such as WAM sander2024watermark . Although these methods share a common abstraction, they are typically trained and deployed as separate, monolithic models with different residual patterns, visual impact, and robustness profiles. This fragmentation is problematic for real systems that must support multiple watermark styles or evolve them over time. A platform or model provider may wish to (i) upgrade an existing watermark to a new design, (ii) interoperate with third-party watermarking schemes, or (iii) offer multiple watermark ``profiles'' (e.g., stronger robustness vs.\ higher visual fidelity) without maintaining separate large models for each. Such changes usually require retraining and redeploying entire encoder-decoder pairs, which can be expensive and brittle hosny2024survey,wang2021survey . In production, however, shipping separate models is costly; a modular framework that supports multiple profiles from a single frozen backbone drastically reduces model loading time and client download sizes, enabling efficient updates without infrastructure overhauls. We study this idea through the lens of adaptability between watermarking models (Figure~ fig:method_overview ). Let be a base encoder and decoder and a target watermarking pair from another method (e.g., TrustMark P/Q, InvisMark, RoSteALS, HiDDeN, or WAM) bui2023trustmark,xu2025invismark,bui2023rosteals,zhu2018hidden,sander2024watermark . We insert a compact adapter into the base models and fine-tune only this adapter, obtaining adapted models that aim to mimic the behavior of on natural images and binary messages. Rather than matching parameters, we define similarity through behavior: encoder adaptation encourages the watermark residuals produced by to match those of and to remain decodable by under standard distortions; decoder adaptation encourages to reliably decode messages embedded by either or . Concretely, we guide adaptation with a novel multi-domain watermark residual alignment loss and a standard BCE secret loss. We use Convolutional-Weight LoRA (CWLoRA), which applies low-rank updates directly to convolutional kernels~ lora . Unlike common post-layer convolutional adapters~ peft,yeh2024navigating,ryu2022diffusionlora , CWLoRA merges into the base weights with no inference-time overhead, and gives the best accuracy/size trade-off in our benchmarks; at rank 16 it needs only 0.9M (encoder) and 2.0M (decoder) parameters, roughly 10 of a typical base model. Across our experiments, CWLoRA adapters closely reproduce target residual patterns (Figure~ fig:residual_grid ) and near-target decoding even across architectures, and the adapted models remain interoperable with the originals: the target decoder can read messages from the adapted encoder and vice versa. Beyond per-method adaptation, we also build a multi-decoder inference pipeline that replaces full decoders with lightweight adapters. Using either an ECC-based (Error Correction Codes) plug-and-play decoder selector or a small classifier-based selector, the adapterized system attains near-oracle decoding accuracy while shrinking total loaded decoder size from 1.2\,GB to 0.14\,GB. With the classifier-based selector, adapterized decoders reach (clean) and (noised), matching/exceeding the original-decoder setting; the ECC-based selector is within 0.6--1.0 of the originals (Table~ tab:multi-dec ). We make the following technical contributions: We formalize cross-method adaptation for neural watermarking via lightweight adapters, proposing objectives for residual alignment and decoder compatibility. We apply Convolutional-Weight LoRA (CWLoRA), a weight-space low-rank adapter for convolutional backbones built on LoRA~ lora , and show it outperforms common post-layer convolutional adapters on this task while introducing no inference-time overhead. We demonstrate effective encoder and decoder adaptation across diverse target watermarks, achieving aligned residuals and near-target decoding despite large architectural differences, and show that these results hold across multiple base methods, out-of-distribution perturbations, and cross-dataset evaluations. We show that CWLoRA on a strong base preserves perceptual quality that full fine-tuning of a comparably small model cannot achieve, confirming that the base's pre-existing priors are essential. We build an adapterized multi-decoder inference pipeline with ECC and classifier-based selection, yielding near-oracle accuracy while reducing the footprint by , enabling flexible deployment from a single base model. Background and Related Work sec:background Image Watermarking. Traditional image watermarking methods operate in spatial or transform domains via spread-spectrum and DCT/DWT-based embedding~ cox1997spread,alhaj2007dwtdct . Most modern methods adopt a neural encoder-decoder trained end-to-end with robustness-oriented noise layers~ zhu2018hidden,jia2021mbrs , sometimes combined with invertible networks for multi-image hiding~ guan2022deepmih . Representative encoder-decoder image schemes include HiDDeN~ zhu2018hidden , StegaStamp~ tancik2020stegastamp , RivaGAN~ zhang2019rivagan , MBRS~ jia2021mbrs , and DeepMIH~ guan2022deepmih , while more recent architectures target arbitrary resolutions and high robustness, such as TrustMark~ bui2023trustmark , RoSteALS~ bui2023rosteals , InvisMark~ xu2025invismark , SynthID gowal2025synthid , and the localized WAM framework~ sander2024watermark . In parallel, in-generation watermarking for generative models operates inside diffusion or autoregressive pipelines~ wen2023treering,yang2024gaussianshading,gunn2025prc,tong2025indexmark,jovanovic2025wmar . Complementary methods such as JIGMark focus on enhancing robustness against specific modifications such as diffusion-based image edits~ pan2024jigmark . Together, these lines of work highlight the diversity of architectures and training recipes, and the lack of a unifying mechanism to make different watermarking styles interoperable at the model level. We use the term watermark adaptation to refer to attempts to make watermarking systems more unified and interoperable across methods, enabling a deployed watermarking stack to accommodate, modify, or switch between different watermark designs without retraining full models. A related but adversarial line of work considers forgery attacks that attempt to mimic the patterns of target watermarks, usually with limited model access saberi2024robustness, yang2024simple, soucek2025transferable . petrov2025coexistence studies the coexistence and ensembling of multiple deep watermarks applied to the same image. Unlike watermark co-existence methods~ petrov2025coexistence , our goal is not to layer multiple methods but to transform one method into another. title: VLAN: Vision-Language Accessible Navigation
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026 Evaluations and Datasets Track. 25 pages, 17 tables, 6 figures. Code: https://github.com/InSAI-Lab/VLAN
summary: Accessible mobility is user-conditioned rather than scene-intrinsic, as walkable paths for one embodiment are inaccessible to another. Yet, existing benchmarks evaluate traversability under a fixed and limited embodiment. We present Vision-Language Accessible Navigation (VLAN), containing 1,000 scenes, 20K navigation trajectories, and 160K keyframes across diverse lighting, environmental conditions, scene semantics, and path geometries. For each trajectory, VLAN provides embodiment-specific actions and accessibility features for legged and wheeled agents, including humanoid and quadruped robots and people with visual or mobility impairments, while everyday obstacles and accessibility labels are categorized as Passable, Bypass, HighRisk, and Blocked. Unlike goal-only evaluation, our benchmark measures physical safety and alignment with user-specific constraints via goal-reaching, collision-aware, and accessibility-aligned metrics. We benchmark modern vision-language models and find they often fail to consistently adapt obstacle relevance, path selection, and safety criteria across user profiles, suggesting accessibility-aware navigation requires dedicated datasets, tasks, and metrics beyond conventional embodied navigation evaluation. All data and code open-source at https://github.com/InSAI-Lab/VLAN.
full_text: Accessible mobility is user-conditioned rather than scene-intrinsic, as walkable paths for one embodiment are inaccessible to another. Yet, existing benchmarks evaluate traversability under a fixed and limited embodiment. We present Vision-Language Accessible Navigation (VLAN), containing 1000 scenes, 20K navigation trajectories, and 160K keyframes across diverse lighting, environmental conditions, scene semantics, and path geometries. For each trajectory, VLAN provides embodiment-specific actions and accessibility features for legged and wheeled agents, including humanoid and quadruped robots and people with visual or mobility impairments, while everyday obstacles and accessibility labels are categorized as Passable, Bypass, HighRisk, and Blocked. Unlike goal-only evaluation, our benchmark measures physical safety and alignment with user-specific constraints via goal-reaching, collision-aware, and accessibility-aligned metrics. We benchmark modern vision-language models and find they often fail to consistently adapt obstacle relevance, path selection, and safety criteria across user profiles, suggesting accessibility-aware navigation requires dedicated datasets, tasks, and metrics beyond conventional embodied navigation evaluation, with all data and code open-source at: . Introduction intro Embodied navigation~ song2025towards, ziliotto2025tango, zheng2024towards, gu2022vision in real-world environments is governed not only by scene geometry and goal location, but also by the physical, perceptual, and operational constraints of the target user or agent. The same obstacle can induce substantially different navigation decisions across embodiments. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:fig1 , a low temporary barrier can be traversable for a humanoid robot, risky for a BVI user, and impassable for a user with mobility impairments. Conversely, overhanging tree branches may have little effect on quadruped robots, yet become critical hazards for drones. These cases highlight a limitation of user-agnostic navigation evaluation, since reaching a target is insufficient if the resulting trajectory is unsafe, inaccessible, or misaligned with the intended user. Existing navigation benchmarks~ ku2020room,krantz_vlnce_2020 have driven substantial progress in vision-language navigation, embodied navigation, and action prediction. However, they typically assume a fixed embodiment and a user-independent traversability criterion, where a trajectory is considered successful if it reaches the target and avoids collisions for a generic agent. This formulation is insufficient for accessibility-aware navigation~ jiang2025bench , where obstacle relevance, safety margins, action granularity, and feasible strategies depend on the target embodiment. Although recent capability-conditioned and embodiment-specific studies~ su2026capnav, windecker2025navitrace, cheng2024navila, wang2024towards have started to examine these differences, existing benchmarks still lack a unified setting for evaluating multiple human and robotic users in the same scenes with user-specific actions and accessibility annotations. Building such a benchmark requires both realistic observations and interactive, editable environments. Real-world videos and street-level imagery capture natural scene appearance, but they are passive and do not readily support scene editing, counterfactual environment modification, action rollout, or collision checking. Simulation provides interactivity and control, but scaling visually diverse and realistic scenes remains costly. Recent work~ xie2025vid2sim, han2025roomtour3d converts monocular videos into photorealistic and physically interactable 3D simulation environments for embodied navigation, enabling reinforcement learning of visual navigation agents in digital twins. Inspired by these works, we find that editable reconstructed scenes can preserve realistic visual appearance while supporting interactive scene modification, trajectory generation, keyframe rendering, and metric-grounded evaluation. Built on these, we present Vision-Language Accessible Navigation (VLAN), a large-scale dataset for evaluating multi-user accessibility-aware navigation. VLAN contains 1,000 scenes, 20K navigation trajectories, and 160K keyframes, spanning diverse lighting, environmental conditions, scene semantics, and path geometries. We provide user-conditioned navigation actions and accessibility annotations for multiple user embodiments, , humanoid robots, quadruped robots, drones, blind or visually impaired (BVI) users, and wheelchair users. This design enables us to generate user-conditioned navigation instances from each scene without relying solely on additional real-world data collection. The drone setting is deliberately formulated as fixed-altitude 2D accessibility-conditioned navigation: the action space is and overhead obstacles are handled by a horizontal detour or a stop, so that the drone and the quadruped robot share one action interface and remain directly comparable on the same scene. Given the same visual path with start-goal pair, VLAN evaluates whether a model can reason and forecast future navigation actions from visual observations and action history for different user embodiments. We propose user-dependent accessibility-aligned metrics, enabling systematic analysis of whether modern vision-language models can adapt obstacle relevance, path selection, safety margins, and action behavior across different users. We instantiate the benchmark with general-purpose vision-language models rather than task-specific navigation agents: existing VLN agents assume a single fixed embodiment and consume an interactive egocentric observation stream, whereas VLAN provides a fixed set of keyframes and requires one model to switch its output modality and safety criteria across five user types. We therefore treat generic VLMs as the appropriate first baseline and expect embodiment-specialised navigation agents to be a natural next step. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce VLAN, a large-scale benchmark for multi-user accessibility-aware navigation with 1,000 scenes, 20K trajectories, and 160K keyframes. For the first time, VLAN involves five embodiments and accessible features for evaluating inclusive navigation. We formulate a user-conditioned navigation setting where the same scene and obstacle layout can induce different navigation actions and accessibility labels for different user embodiments, , humanoid robots, quadruped robots, drones, blind or visually impaired (BVI) users, and wheelchair users. We provide user-specific actions, obstacle categories, accessibility labels, and collision-aware evaluation protocols for assessing large vision-language models beyond goal-reaching performance. We benchmark modern vision-language models and show that current systems struggle to consistently adapt navigation behavior and safety criteria across user profiles. Related Work related and capability-conditioned navigation. Vision-language navigation benchmarks such as R2R~ anderson2018vision , RxR~ ku2020room , and VLN-CE~ krantz_vlnce_2020 have advanced instruction-following navigation from discrete graph settings to continuous embodied environments. Recent work explores long-horizon VLN and scalable task generation~ song2025towards . However, most benchmarks assume a fixed embodiment and a user-independent notion of traversability. Capability- and embodiment-conditioned studies begin to address this limitation. CapNav~ su2026capnav evaluates VLMs under agent-specific mobility constraints, NaviTrace~ windecker2025navitrace studies embodiment-conditioned image-space navigation traces, and VLN-PE~ wang2025rethinking analyzes the physical and visual gaps in cross-embodiment VLN. Platform-specific work on legged robots and UAVs further shows that different agents require different action spaces and obstacle constraints~ cheng2024navila,wang2024towards . EmbodiedCity~ gao2024embodiedcity and Embodied4C~ sohn2025embodied4c further introduce embodiment shifts across vehicles, drones, and manipulators, but remain robot- or vehicle-centric: they include no human users with perceptual or mobility impairments, no user-conditioned accessibility labels, and no test of whether a model produces different outputs for different users given identical visual input. VLAN differs by evaluating multiple human and robotic users in the same scenes with user-specific actions, accessibility labels, and safety-aware metrics. and accessibility-aware benchmarks. Recent assistive benchmarks evaluate VLMs for visually impaired assistance and human-centered perception. VIALM shows that large models can lack environment grounding and fine-grained guidance for visually impaired users~ zhao2024vialm . @BENCH~ jiang2025bench evaluates VLMs on assistive tasks selected by people with visual impairments, including segmentation, depth estimation, OCR, captioning, and VQA. WalkVLM~ yuan2025walkvlm constructs a video-based benchmark for visually impaired walking assistance. These works emphasize accessibility-aware reasoning, but they are largely perception-, description-, or reminder-oriented. VLAN instead provides an action-level and instruction-level navigation benchmark with goal-reaching, collision-aware, and accessibility-aligned evaluation. -to-interactive simulation for navigation. Videos are visually diverse but passive, while simulation enables interaction but is costly to scale with realistic scenes. Established embodied platforms~ savva2019habitat provide control and photorealistic rendering but still require hand-built 3D assets. RoomTour3D~ han2025roomtour3d constructs geometry-aware video-instruction data from web-based room tour videos, while Vid2Sim~ xie2025vid2sim converts monocular videos into photorealistic and physically interactable simulation environments for urban navigation. EmbodiedSplat~ chhablani2025embodiedsplat , GaussGym~ escontrela2025gaussgym , and RoboGSim~ li2024robogsim further explore Gaussian-splatting-based interactive environments for robot learning and evaluation. VLAN builds on this direction for a different purpose, using editable reconstructed scenes to construct a scalable multi-user accessibility-aware navigation benchmark. VLAN Dataset and Benchmark sec:dataset VLAN is a large-scale benchmark for multi-user accessibility-aware navigation. It contains 1,000 scenes, 20K navigation trajectories, and 160K keyframes. Each scene contains about 20 trajectories, and each trajectory is represented by eight keyframes. For each trajectory, VLAN provides visual observations, camera poses, obstacle metadata, accessibility labels, and user-conditioned navigation targets. The benchmark is designed to evaluate whether models can adapt navigation behavior to different user embodiments under the same visual scene, start-goal pair, and obstacle layout. Dataset Construction and Diversity subsec:dataset_construction reconstruction and editing. VLAN is constructed from egocentric scene videos and associated navigation routes. Fig.~ fig:data_pipe summarizes the overall pipeline from video collection to Gaussian reconstruction~ li2025streamgs, wang2024vggsfm, xie2025vid2sim , Unity-based scene editing, trajectory generation, and sample construction. We first reconstruct each scene into a Gaussian-splat representation and import the reconstructed scene into Unity~ juliani2018unity for controlled editing. Instead of treating captured environments as fixed visual observations, VLAN uses reconstructed scenes as interactive and editable environments. This design preserves realistic visual appearance while enabling systematic variation of scene states, route conditions, and obstacle configurations. As shown in Fig.~ fig:scene_edit , the same reconstructed scene can be assigned different traffic-light states and modified with different obstacle configurations.
